sources.title: OpenAI appoints Dan Driscoll as Senior Counselor for National Security Modernization

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: OpenAI hires former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll for national security role
sources.text: OpenAI has hired former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll as senior counselor for national security modernization, a newly created role at the company . Driscoll will focus on how artificial intelligence can be used to strengthen U.S. national security and cybersecurity, OpenAI said, while his updated LinkedIn profile also lists his new position. He will work with OpenAI's senior leadership and external partners, with a particular focus on helping U.S. allies adopt advanced AI responsibly. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the U.S. has "an extraordinary opportunity to work with other countries to spread the adoption of democratic AI," and that Driscoll's appointment would help strengthen American leadership in the technology. "National security requirements are changing faster than at any time in the past fifty years," Driscoll said. He added that AI could help reduce paperwork, process information and deliver answers more quickly to those working in national security. The appointment comes after Driscoll stepped down as Army secretary earlier this year after months of reported tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. An Iraq war veteran, Driscoll pushed efforts to modernize the U.S. military, including expanding access to drone and counter-drone technologies among U.S. allies, according to a previous U.S. Army announcement. Driscoll also met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv in November 2025 to discuss a U.S.-proposed peace plan aimed at ending the war with Russia, according to a statement from the Presidential Office of Ukraine. At OpenAI, Driscoll will work with government officials, industry leaders, academic institutions and allied organizations to advance what the company calls "democratic AI." He will also help internal teams understand the operational needs of national security institutions, building on OpenAI's efforts to strengthen cyber resilience and protect essential services through its Daybreak program .

sources.title: Google fine-tunes its Agentic Data Cloud to support highly scalable autonomous AI workers
sources.text: Artificial intelligence is no longer just about conversational assistants that tell people what to do. These days, it’s all about work automation, and Google Cloud is making sure it’s right at the forefront of that trend with its revamped Agentic Data Cloud platform, which received a host of new updates today. The Agentic Data Cloud was launched earlier this year at Google Cloud Next. It’s meant to be the architectural “system of action” for AI agents , replacing the brittle extract, transform and load-based data pipelines, or ETL, that feed legacy software applications. The key advantage of Agentic Data Cloud is that it meets customers where their data is, so rather than forcing them to squeeze all of their information in a large, centralized data warehouse, it enables AI agents to access it wherever it lives. In a blog post, Sirish Chandrasekaran, Google’s vice president of product management for data analytics, outlined the company’s belief that autonomous agents rather than humans will soon become the primary consumers of data. As such, it makes sense to build a purpose-built infrastructure stack specifically for them, prioritizing low latency, zero data movement and automated governance. “That is why we built the Agentic Data Cloud — a system of action designed to activate all your data by breaking down walled gardens, deliver high accuracy and trust, and operate proactively at low cost,” Chandrasekaran said. The flagship new feature in Agentic Data Cloud is borderless Lakehouse , a special version of Google’s “cross-border Lakehouse” product that also debuted at Cloud Next. Chandrasekaran said borderless Lakehouse is built upon the open-source Apache Iceberg table format and designed to eliminate multicloud friction with new caching capabilities for Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure. This allows companies to query remote data held in those cloud platforms over a secure private link, without having to pay egress fees. Chandrasekaran detailed how it works, saying that it automatically caches retrieved data blocks within Google Cloud to accelerate subsequent queries. There’s also a new AlloyDB integration that allows users to query external Iceberg tables with standard PostgreSQL queries without having to copy data. In this way, it bridges real-time transactional data with historical lakehouse records. One of the big problems with autonomous agents is that they can be prone to hallucinations without proper guardrails in place, which is why Google has overhauled another capability within Agentic Data Cloud. The Knowledge Catalog , which is a kind of map of business meaning that’s meant to inform AI agents of the peculiarities of the organization they work for, is getting a new self-learning enrichment capability in preview. According to Chandrasekaran, it works by continuously scanning unstructured data in Google Workspace, Jira, SharePoint and GitHub to translate operational knowledge into Open Knowledge Format context sets. These can be used to ground AI agents in organizational knowledge, and the results from early adopters shows that it can help make the average agent four-times more accurate, while reducing token consumption by up to 75%. Knowledge Catalog is seen as so important to Google’s agentic future that it’s also being enabled by default in the Gemini application starting today. Because it’s so tightly integrated, it can resolve issues around business metric definitions and access controls before it translates user’s prompts into Structured Query Language queries. Companies can also choose to ground agents in semantic models for specific data platforms, including Google BigQuery, Snowflake, SAP, Looker and dbt. “Agents are only as accurate as the business context they’re grounded in,” Chandrasekaran said. “Whether an agent is calculating net revenue for finance or customer churn for operations, it applies the exact same governed formulas your business teams rely on.” Gemini is also getting new autonomous machine learning capabilities that can help to streamline everyday work for both technical teams and business workers. For instance, data engineers can now tell Gemini a specific business outcome they want to achieve in natural language, and Gemini will generate the PySpark code, run the notebooks and fix any data pipeline errors as it works toward that goal. Meanwhile, business users will be able to generate reliable, real-time operational reports in Gemini simply by asking for them. “Gemini uses operational reporting skills integrated with BigQuery and the Knowledge Catalog to construct and save the query,” Chandrasekaran explained. “Once saved, teams can run reports on demand without incurring token costs, guaranteeing consistent and verified answers every time.” Google also has a few gifts for software developers, starting with the new Data Agent Kit , which is generally available from today, bringing Model Context Protocol tooling into integrated development environments such as VS Code, Claude Code and Antigravity . This means that developers can now just define their business intent in natural language and have agents automatically create, fine-tune and test the associated data pipelines. Developers can also take advantage of infrastructure updates that are designed to facilitate “high-concurrency agent interactions,” so that thousands of AI agents can query the same database simultaneously without swamping it and causing problems. These include the broader preview of AlloyDB Express , a highly scalable database that supports sub-two-second provisioning for rapid agent prototyping. There’s also PostgreSQL for agents in AlloyDB , which provides an isolated workload environment that can handle three million queries per second. Finally, Google said BigQuery Graph is now generally available, bringing petabyte-scale graph analytics into relational database tables with zero ETL. It’s joined by previews of the TimesFM 3.0 forecasting model and TabFM predictive analyt

sources.name: TechCrunch AI
sources.title: AI inference startup Fal doubles its valuation to $16B as demand surges
sources.text: Fal , a San Francisco-based startup that hosts and runs AI video, image, and audio models, has raised $1.3 billion in its latest funding round led by Bessemer Venture Partners, with participation from Nvidia, Sound Ventures, and T. Rowe Price. The deal values Fal at $16 billion, double its $8 billion valuation in April, Bloomberg reported . The startup announced its Series E and F rounds at the same time, noting that a combined $1.65 billion was raised across both. (Sequoia led the earlier round.) The latest round (Series F) comes amid soaring demand for inference services, the process of running an AI model that’s already been trained to generate outputs, particularly from customers relying on open source models. Fal surpassed $800 million in annualized revenue earlier this year, Bloomberg’s report noted. Companies providing inference services, including Baseten, Fireworks AI, and Modal, have also been growing rapidly and raising large funding rounds at higher valuations . But their gross margins remain thin because of the high cost of buying or leasing compute, according to several people familiar with inference companies’ financials. Fal was co-founded in 2021 by Burkay Gur, a former Coinbase machine learning leader and Oracle engineer, and Gorkem Yurtseven, who was previously a developer at Amazon. sources.title: Generative media inference startup fal raises $1.3B at a $16B valuation
sources.text: Generative media inference startup fal today announced it has raised $1.3 billion in new funding at a valuation of $16 billion, according to Bloomberg. The company will spend the money on computing power and on hiring beyond its current 185 employees. Fal provides a cloud platform for running image, video and audio generation models, and developers reach all of them through a single application programming interface. Entertainment studios, advertising agencies and game developers are among the customers using those models in production, according to the company. In-house researchers also post-train some of those models to run faster. Over the past year that work has centered on video, in partnership with the open- and closed-source developers that build the models. Some of the deals pay fal licensing fees or a share of revenue, Bloomberg reported. Co-founder and Chief Executive Burkay Gur told the outlet the round is as large as it is because demand has surged and serving it takes more compute. “We hit a point in summer where we were not able to serve our customers and had to rate-limit them,” he said. Pretraining a model of fal’s own is not on the near-term agenda, said Gur, who did not rule it out for later. Annualized revenue at fal passed $800 million earlier this year, a person familiar with the matter told Bloomberg. The valuation puts fal just behind rival inference provider Fireworks AI Inc., which closed $1.5 billion in funding at a $17.5 billion valuation in July . Several people familiar with the finances of inference companies told TechCrunch that gross margins across the sector remain thin because compute is expensive to buy or lease. Gur started the company in 2021 with Chief Technology Officer Gorkem Yurtseven. His resume includes leading machine learning work at Coinbase Global Inc. and an engineering role at Oracle Corp. Yurtseven was previously a developer at Amazon.com Inc. Bessemer Venture Partners led the Series F round, and its partner Talia Goldberg is joining the board of Features & Labels Inc., as fal is formally known. Nvidia Corp., Sound Ventures, HOF Capital and T. Rowe Price Group Inc. also participated. Fal described Nvidia as a strategic investor. Today’s announcement also covered an April round led by Sequoia Capital. That Series E round raised $350 million at an $8 billion valuation, per Bloomberg, and fal said the two rounds come to $1.65 billion combined. Last December , the company raised $140 million at a $4.5 billion valuation. Investors have now put more than $1.9 billion into the company. sources.name: The Guardian Technology
sources.title: Google says there’s no way to use Search without using artificial intelligence
sources.text: In announcement geared to schools, tech giant shows how entwined AI is with the world’s most popular website Google just acknowledged that you can’t use Google Search without using artificial intelligence . The search giant announced a slate of new AI products for classrooms and schools on Tuesday as well as more ways for teachers and schools to limit or restrict use of those AI tools. The company said the schools should have control over whether students use AI in the classroom. There’s one catch, though: if a school or teacher blocks the use of Google’s AI features, students won’t be able to use Google Search. “After listening to schools, teachers, leading researchers, and policymakers, we are now updating our approach to controls for Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search,” company executives wrote in a blogpost. “Access to these products will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on.” In a comment to the New York Times , Chris Phillips, Google’s vice-president for education, said that there is no Google Search without AI. “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” said Phillips. A school-wide ban on AI would mean that students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available”, he told the Times. The Guardian also reached out to Google but did not hear back by publication. To some, the move reads like a penalty for not implementing Google’s AI features. New York City’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, who recently imposed a one-year moratorium on generative AI tools in city schools through the eighth grade, said Google was exploiting its near-total control of online search. “Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools,” Mamdani posted on X. “No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children. Our public schools exist to serve students, not to grow the profit margins of Big Tech.” Lina Khan, former chair of the US Federal Trade Commission, echoed his statement, tweeting that Google was using its monopoly on search to “to coerce schools into adopting AI”. The ubiquity of Google Search has long made it a critical tool for students, and losing access to it may prove enough of a reason to opt in to using new AI features for schools. Google has also maintained a stranglehold on technology in US classrooms for years by offering cheap and free products. From Gmail and Google Docs to Google Classroom and Google Chromebooks, the company’s suite of software and hardware solutions are among the most widely used in schools. One of the new features Google announced today was Guided Learning, an AI study tool that “coaches students through the process of problem solving” rather than giving them the answer. The company is planning to integrate Guided Learning directly into Google Search. “For example, if a student pastes a complex physics problem or asks for help writing a book report in Search, they’ll see prompts to help them think critically and work through the concepts, without going directly to the answer,” the company wrote in a blogpost. Lila Byock, founder of Schools Beyond Screens, called Google’s announcement a “hostile ultimatum”. Schools Beyond Screens is a national coalition of parents and teachers advocating for more student-centered policies on the use of screens in schools. “This kind of bullying has no place in our schools,” Byock said in a statement. “Educational value – not shareholder value – must determine which products are used by students and regulators must intervene to prevent big tech from exploiting schoolchildren for profit.”

sources.name: The Verge AI
sources.title: OpenAI says ChatGPT is catching up to Google in search
sources.text: ChatGPT processes one-fifth the volume of search queries as Google, per OpenAI. ChatGPT processes one-fifth the volume of search queries as Google, per OpenAI. In many circles, “Ask Chat” has replaced “Google it,” and that’s reflected in a new announcement from OpenAI: the volume of search queries run through ChatGPT now equals 20 percent of the volume run through Google. Adam Fry, OpenAI’s consumer product lead for ChatGPT, made the announcement at a press event on Monday. He said the company defines a search as any time a user inputs a query that results in a web search, as opposed to tasks like defining a term or a simple how-to explanation. (Fry did not specify the source of the Google search volume number.) Having one-fifth as many searches as Google is still a long way from overtaking it, but for comparison, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said during Google’s 2023 antitrust trial that Bing had about 3 percent of the search engine market share after trying for more than a decade. During the trial, Google described AI as a potential disruptor, arguing ChatGPT was poised to seriously compete with it — now, OpenAI seems to agree. (OpenAI likely uses Microsoft Bing for a significant part of its searches, along with its in-house search index, although there is still some speculation that it routes some queries through Google.) The news comes amid an ongoing search engine shake-up, as Google continues to reduce conventional referrals to third-party sites and invests heavily in AI tools — not just AI Overview but also additional generative AI capabilities , including personalized search results with visualizations and charts. But as search queries increasingly route through OpenAI and other AI labs’ services, other companies are investing in the same types of AI-focused search experience, even if they call it something else: for OpenAI, it’s “Intelligent UI,” or creating a visual and interactive interface within a chatbot response. “That’s where the future of this technology goes. You’re talking to a canvas,” Fry said. Much like Google, OpenAI sees a potential path to profitability through ads, particularly as it approaches an IPO potentially slated for early next year. OpenAI has defended its ads in the past, and Fry told reporters they hadn’t produced a lasting backlash. “Ads have not negatively impacted the product or the usage of the product,” he said, adding that “most people do not seem to mind ads in the product.” OpenAI announced last month that the company would begin introducing images of sponsored products and services in ChatGPT rather than just a company’s name, logo, and a link to its product like before. “Ads have maybe shown us that we could be doing this more, actually,” Fry said.

stories.title: AMD's data center revenue nearly doubles in Q3 and CEO Su expects growth to accelerate
stories.summary: AMD reported better-than-expected third-quarter results, driven by booming sales of AI chips

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: AMD's data center revenue nearly doubles in Q3 and CEO Su expects growth to accelerate
sources.text: Advanced Micro Devices reported third-quarter earnings on Tuesday that beat Wall Street's expectations, with revenue jumping 45% and data center sales nearly doubling from a year earlier. The stock was up 8% in extended trading, but later pared those gains as election results came in. Here's how the chipmaker did versus LSEG consensus estimates for the quarter: Revenue increased from $9.25 billion a year earlier, AMD said in a statement . Neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius rallied earlier Tuesday and remained higher after AMD reported results. CEO Lisa Su said on the earnings call that she expects server revenue to double year over year in 2027 and data center AI growth to accelerate even faster than the company had projected 90 days ago. The company expects data center to drive the majority of its revenue and earnings growth. "We have worked across our supply chain to secure the wafers, substrates, advanced packaging, memory, and other key components needed to support much higher growth next year," Su said on the earnings call. AMD's report comes days after Intel disclosed similar data center growth, with revenue in that segment up 78% in the third quarter. But Intel's stock plummeted 29% on Friday over concerns about weak guidance and Intel's ability to meet demand . The data center unit makes up the majority of AMD's business, accounting for 64% of overall revenue, up from 47% a year ago. After years spent chasing Nvidia in the market for artificial intelligence graphics processing units, or GPUs, AMD's central processing units, or CPUs, are experiencing a major resurgence with the rise of agentic AI apps like Meta 's Muse. AMD's server CPUs are key for agentic apps because they power virtual machines and can run for hours on their own. Demand from agentic AI boosted AMD shares to a record in October. "Adoption is just starting, and we expect demand to grow sharply as agents are deployed more broadly and take on more complex work," Su said on the earnings call with analysts. AMD's stock is up about 125% this year, but it saw three consecutive days of losses before rallying on Tuesday amid an industrywide sell-off tied to fears about overspending on AI. AMD is also a major player in the weakening PC market, which Intel blamed for its poor outlook last week. AMD and Intel are the largest makers of traditional x86 processors that power many laptops and desktops, while other laptops rely on Arm -based processors from the likes of Qualcomm and Apple. Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter from a year earlier due to soaring costs for memory and other components, according to Counterpoint Research . AMD reports PC chip sales in a segment combined with gaming chips. Revenue in that business fell 8% from a year earlier to $3.7 billion. Gaming revenue was down 40% from a year ago. For the fourth quarter, AMD said it expects about $17 billion in revenue, beating the $16.2 billion average analyst estimate, according to LSEG. AMD sees its gross margin for the quarter coming in at 55%, slightly below the average estimate of 55.3%, according to StreetAccount. AMD also sells data center GPUs and full rack-scale systems called Helios that compete directly with Nvidia's Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems. Meta, Microsoft , Anthropic, OpenAI, and Oracle are all beginning to use AMD Helios in their data centers. Meta said last week that its Helios racks are up and running, and AMD agreed to invest $1 billion in Meta's equity offering. AMD has also committed to investing up to $5 billion in Anthropic, which unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week as it inches closer to a potentially historic initial public offering . During a visit to Taiwan in October, Su said she plans to "substantially increase our supply in 2027." Su and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have both made multiple trips to Taiwan and South Korea this year, holding meetings with key suppliers like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and memory leaders SK Hynix and Samsung. In September, AMD said it would acquire World Labs for $8.2 billion in an all-stock deal. The San Francisco-based AI lab, founded by industry pioneer Fei-Fei Li, is developing a so-called world model that simulates 3D environments to aid in developing robots and other physically grounded AI applications. sources.name: SiliconANGLE
sources.title: AMD beats expectations as agentic AI sparks its data center revenue growth engines
sources.text: Shares of the chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices Inc. rose more than 5% in late trading today after it delivered solid third-quarter earnings and revenue today, with data center sales almost doubling from a year ago. The company reported earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $2.09 per share, easily beating Wall Street’s forecast of $1.95 per share. Revenue for the period jumped 45% from a year earlier, to $13.38 billion, ahead of the $13.09 billion analyst consensus estimate. All told, the company’s net income for the quarter came to $3.47 billion, up 77% from the previous year when it posted a profit of just $1.96 billion. The star performer in the quarter was AMD’s data center business unit, which accounted for 64% of its overall revenue, up from just 47% one year ago. After spending years trying to compete with Nvidia Corp.’s graphics processing units for artificial intelligence market share, the company’s traditional central processing units or CPUs are suddenly back in vogue thanks to the emergence of agentic AI applications such as Meta Platforms Inc.’s Muse. Autonomous AI agents can run much more efficiently on CPUs than they can on GPUs, boosting demand for the chips. Looking ahead, AMD expects its server revenue to double year-over-year in fiscal 2027, with AI growth likely to accelerate even faster than the company projected just three months ago. “Adoption is just starting and we expect demand to grow sharply as agents are deployed more broadly and take on more complex work,” AMD Chief Executive Lisa Su (pictured) said on a conference call with analysts. AMD’s data center story isn’t all about CPUs, though. The company also sells GPUs, including bundles of them shipped inside data center-ready rack-scale systems called Helios, and that system’s popularity is growing fast. Su said Anthropic PBC, OpenAI Group PBC, Microsoft Corp., Oracle Corp. and Meta are all using AMD Helios systems in their data centers. Last week, Meta said its first Helion racks are already up and running as it revealed that AMD invested $1 billion in its latest equity offering. The chipmaker has also committed to a $5 billion investment in Anthropic, which last week revealed the long-awaited prospectus for its upcoming initial public offering. AMD delivered its latest earnings report just days after its rival Intel Corp. did the same. Intel also posted strong data center revenue growth, but its stock fell more than 30% on Friday on weak guidance and concerns about its ability to meet demand for its products. But Su said AMD had no such problems. Last month she made a high-profile visit to Taiwan, where she held meetings with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. and a number of supply chain partners, and said after the trip that the company plans to substantially increase its supply in the coming year. “We have worked across our supply chain to secure the wafers, substrates, advanced packaging, memory and other key components needed to support much higher growth next year,” Su added. AMD’s results will go some way toward reassuring investors who have become increasingly nervous about the direction of the AI industry and whether the hundreds of billions of dollars being spent on it each year is actually going to generate a return on their investments, said eMarketer analyst Jacob Bourne. “The results are a test of AMD’s own performance and the broader AI trade, and its data center and revenue beats will encourage investors after the recent semiconductor selloff,” he added. Though AMD is far from immune to the recent volatility that has afflicted AI-related stocks, its future still looks increasingly rosy for now. “Demand for AI computing is not going to fall off a cliff, and AMD has the competitive products and major customer relationships to capitalize on that demand,” Bourne said. Strength in the data center unit is helping AMD to ride out difficulties in its traditional market for personal computers, which is the reason for Intel’s poor outlook. During the second quarter, global PC shipments fell 4% from a year earlier, with buyers dissuaded by the rising cost of components such as memory chips, according to data from Counterpoint Research. Along with Intel, AMD is a leading manufacturer of the x86 CPUs that power most of the world’s computers and laptops. The company reports PC chip revenue within a segment that also includes its chips for games consoles, and that unit saw its revenue decline 8% from a year earlier, to $3.7 billion. Gaming revenue fell 40% from the previous year. For the current quarter, AMD is targeting revenue of abouot $17 billion at the midpoint of its guidance range, ahead of the Street’s $16.2 billion consensus estimate. The company also sees its gross margins coming in at 55%, just below the Street’s forecast of 55.3%. AMD was busy on the acquisition front during the quarter. In September it revealed it’s going to buy World Labs Inc. for $8.2 billion in an all-stock deal. The San Francisco-based AI lab, founded by the AI industry luminary Fei-Fei Li, has developed world models that can simulate 3D environments to support the training of intelligent robots and other physical AI applications. The company also acquired a startup called Taalas Inc. that makes specialized model-specific integrated circuits, which are essentially chips that can be customized to run a specific AI model more efficiently. That acquisition should help to boost AMD’s position in AI inference. AMD also invested in the AI image generation model maker Stability AI Ltd., which raised $76 million in funding in August. sources.name: The Verge AI
sources.title: Data centers lost the midterms
sources.text: In ballot measures and exit polls, voters across the country rejected unrestrained development.﻿ In ballot measures and exit polls, voters across the country rejected unrestrained development.﻿ Data center developers are poised to face a more restrictive building environment after voters across the country voted in candidates who favor moratoriums and ballot measures that put more obstacles on their expansion, delivering a stinging blow to a central pillar of the AI industry. Of voters polled by NBC News on Election Day, 76 percent said they opposed data centers in their communities. Dozens of local communities voted directly to restrict development through ballot measures . And upset winners like Texas Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa and Michigan’s Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed support moratoriums on development. It’s hard to draw a direct line from data center backlash to the election of any of these candidates, and there were still some races where candidates who favored more limited restrictions on data centers prevailed. Republican Rep. Byron Donalds, who previously lauded development in Florida, was elected as governor, and Iowa’s Democratic Governor-elect Rob Sand opposed a moratorium that his challenger favored. But even these candidates were forced to engage on data center issues during their campaigns, and will be likely to face continued pressure to put at least some guardrails in place. Voters were faced with questions about data centers directly in 45 local ballot measures nationwide. As of Wednesday morning, according to a site compiled by Redbud Consulting , the results of 33 of those will restrict data center development. The Town of Wells, Maine, favored a 180-day moratorium on large data centers, backdated to mid-June 2026. Several cities in Ohio voted to ban data centers over 25MW. The City of El Dorado, Kansas , voted to ban data centers with peak electrical load over 10MW for 10 years. Dozens of local communities voted directly to restrict development Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa will take over the governor’s seat from Republican incumbent Greg Abbott, marking a major Democratic flip in a state with the second-highest number of planned data centers. Hinojosa supports a statewide moratorium on data center development , while Abbott took a more measured approach. He announced a new audit this summer on data centers that could slow new developments from connecting to the state energy grid, but has previously praised data center expansion in the state. In another major upset, Democratic State Rep. James Talarico flipped Texas blue in a landmark Senate victory against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. Both Talarico and Paxton wanted to remove some tax exemptions for data centers, and to make them responsible for their own energy infrastructure-related costs. But Talarico also put an emphasis on the facilities’ environmental impact and ensuring they shared their profits with the public, while Paxton’s message focused on keeping Chinese tech out of data centers. Republican congressman Byron Donalds won the governor’s seat over Democratic former congressman David Jolly. Donalds opposed an outright ban of data centers, while Jolly said he’d bar hyperscalers for a year beginning on day one in office. In Congress, Donalds introduced the Protecting Ratepayers Act, which would make developers pay for their own energy and water needs. Donalds’ win was still closer than expected in a state that’s been a Republican stronghold in the Trump era. As of Wednesday morning, NBC News reported that Donalds had exactly 50 percent of the vote, with 99 percent of expected votes already counted, while Jolly had 48.7 percent, and the rest went to an Independent candidate. Democratic incumbent Governor Josh Shapiro held onto his seat against Republican challenger and state Treasurer Stacy Garrity. Both Shapiro and Garrity toughened their stances against data centers as the race went on, despite previously touting their potential benefits to the state. Shapiro signed an executive order that barred nondisclosure agreements for data center developments and took proposals for AI data centers off the fast track. Garrity has said she supports a development pause of up to three years. Democrat Sherrod Brown won back his former Senate seat from Republican incumbent Jon Husted, whom Brown had labeled “the face of data centers.” The National Republican Senatorial Committee warned this summer in a leaked memo that if data centers were blamed for Husted’s potential loss, it would make them seem poisonous to future candidates. Husted earlier helped install data center tax breaks as lieutenant governor, though he more recently introduced the Ratepayer Protection Act in Congress to force large data centers to cover their infrastructure upgrade and energy costs. Brown hammered Husted on the issue throughout the campaign, and while he hasn’t gone as far as to call for a moratorium , he’s said that developers shouldn’t get tax breaks or get a go-ahead without local input. Mike Rogers. sources.title: The Results Are In: Voters Hate Data Centers
sources.text: It was a bad night for data centers . In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown, who has aired ads for months calling his opponent “the face of data centers in Ohio,” cruised to victory to flip a Senate seat. Democrat Chris Pappas, who when seated will be the nation’s first openly gay male senator, mentioned his opposition to data centers in his victory speech and drew massive boos from his crowd in New Hampshire—even though the state has no large-scale data centers under construction. Elsewhere, two separate Republicans named Derek and Derrick, whose Democratic opponents labeled them “Data Center Derek” and “DC Derrick,” suffered losses in House races in Ohio and Wisconsin. As part of last night’s shocking blue tsunami , voters selected candidates with tough policies on data centers at all levels of government, in a clear rebuke to the industry’s buildout in states across the country. Almost a quarter of all voters told NBC News that data centers were “crucial” to their vote, while nearly two-thirds said it was either a major or minor factor. “The revolt against data centers was one of the top issues of the 2026 election, and in a few years we will look back on it as just the early tremor of a much bigger AI earthquake upending American politics,” Greg Casar, the Texas Democratic congressman, said in a statement . “Data centers and AI as a technology are fundamentally linked in many voters' minds,” says Alexander McCoy, a Democratic strategist working on AI. “So you can address all of the different concerns with data centers with regards to their energy or their noise, or their pollution, and there would still be significant concerns about what these projects are enabling and the effect is having on opportunities, prices, jobs, society.” Perhaps some of the biggest shocks for the industry came in the governor’s mansions. In stunning upsets, voters elected Democrats Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia and Gina Hinojosa in Texas, while putting Cindy Holscher on the cusp of a potential win in Kansas. All of these candidates campaigned not just for increased regulations on the industry, but for data center moratoriums. A pause on data centers in Texas and Georgia especially, two of the biggest hubs for development in the country, could have serious implications for the hundreds of projects planned for each of those states. “I think we will see the end to favorable tax breaks, and it’s clear that people like Greg Abbott were harmed by their history of giving those financial incentives to AI companies and data center developers,” says McCoy. “I think we'll likely see the appointment of regulators in various administrative bureaucratic bodies that pose more scrutiny on these projects and an increase in the enforcement of environmental protection regulations.” Simply being anti-data center wasn’t enough to boost some candidates—especially Republicans. In Wisconsin, Republican Tom Tiffany, who hit Democrat David Crowley early on in his campaign with ads dubbing him “Data Center David Crowley,” lost his race. (Crowley got more aggressive on the industry as the campaign went on, indicating he would support a pause two weeks before election day.) So did incumbent Mike Lawler in New York’s 17th congressional district, who aired ads slamming his opponent’s past statements that New York “needs” data centers, conceded his race even though the Associated Press has yet to call it. Throughout the campaign, data centers proved to be a bipartisan topic of concern , and caused fractures within the parties themselves. Earlier this year, WIRED reported how many of Donald Trump’s MAGA loyalists disagreed with the president’s support for AI companies and data centers. But it’s undeniable that anger about data centers helped elect Democrats. In the weeks leading up to the elections, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee ran ads that highlighted Republicans’ support for data centers or the backing they had received from AI companies. “Voters aren’t stupid. The data center story is a corruption story. It's an affordability story. It's a Big Tech CEOs influence story,” says Sacha Haworth executive director of the Tech Oversight Project. “That's what voters understood when they cast their ballots and that's why Democrats routed Republicans so, so hard last night, because Republicans could not tell the same story.” Many of the candidates who won on stricter data center regulations did so despite massive injections of cash from the AI and data center industries to their opponents. In South Carolina, Building the Future, a new industry super PAC, spent $1.5 million to support Darline Graham; she lost last night to Democrat Annie Andrews, who favors a moratorium. (Andrews registered the URL DataCenterDarline.com in late September to hit Graham on her industry connections.) Building the Future also injected more than $1.5 million into the Kansas gubernatorial race to support Republican Ty Masterson against Holscher. And Michigan Democrat Will Lawrence, who made regulations on AI and data centers a cornerstone of his campaign, has declared victory (though without an AP announcement) over Republican Tom Barrett in one of the most expensive races in the country. Barrett had gotten $340,000 from Elon Musk’s America PAC over the course of the race. “Despite poll after poll making it clear that the conservative rural working-class base was concerned about data centers and the impact of AI, too many politicians in Washington chose big AI’s money over their own base,” Amy Kremer, chair of Humans First, an advocacy group pushing for democratic oversight of AI, said in a statement. In data center ballot measures across nine states, voters rejected future construction plans, approved moratoriums, and called for greater consultation with and accountability to local communities.
